evidence.label: Invariant-projection counterexamples for every irrational rotation
Backward intertwiners and a transitive commutant

headline: Proves that some operators on Hilbert space have no hyperinvariant subspace, a negative answer to a long-open problem.
scope: Bounded operators on separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces, plus weighted rotations in the hyperfinite II₁ factor for each irrational angle.
plain: An operator is a linear map on an infinite-dimensional space. A hyperinvariant subspace is a proper closed piece of the space that every map commuting with the operator keeps inside itself. The hyperinvariant-subspace problem asked whether every non-scalar operator has one. Two companion papers build a nonzero operator that has none, and Lean checks this. The operator still has many ordinary invariant subspaces, so the related invariant-subspace problem stays open.
doesNot: This does not settle the invariant-subspace problem: the operator built here still has many ordinary invariant subspaces.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Douglas and Pearcy, who studied the link between hyperinvariant subspaces and transitive algebras
scorecard.significanceWhy: It gives a negative answer, with a Lean check, to the hyperinvariant-subspace problem of operator theory.

explanation:
Start in two dimensions. Let T send the vector (a, b) to (a, 2b). The vectors (a, 0) are stretched by 1, and the vectors (0, b) by 2. Suppose a map A commutes with T, so AT = TA. Take v = (1, 0), so Tv = v. Then T(Av) = A(Tv) = Av, so Av is again stretched by 1. So every map that commutes with T keeps the line of vectors (a, 0) inside itself.

That line is a hyperinvariant subspace. A subspace is a flat piece of the space through zero. It is invariant for a map if the map keeps it inside itself. It is hyperinvariant if every map that commutes with T keeps it inside itself. In finite dimensions, any non-scalar map has such a piece, built from its eigenvectors, the vectors it only stretches. A scalar map just multiplies everything by one number.

In an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, a space of infinite sequences with a notion of length, that argument can fail. The hyperinvariant-subspace problem asks whether every bounded non-scalar operator there has a nonzero proper closed hyperinvariant subspace[3]. The hard cases are quasinilpotent operators. These are operators whose powers shrink faster than any geometric rate, and they may have no eigenvectors at all. An earlier preprint claiming the problem was equivalent to the invariant-subspace problem was withdrawn after a counterexample[9].

The second paper answers the problem negatively[1]. Its operator S shifts each basis vector one step and scales it by a positive weight. Its norm, the most it stretches any vector, is e^−10. The norm of its n-th power is at most e^−10·k, where k is the whole part of (n + 1)²/4[2]. For n = 3, k = 4, so S³ shrinks lengths by at least e^−40. The n-th root of that bound is e^−40/3, about 0.0000016. For n = 9, k = 25 and the root is e^−250/9, about 8 × 10^−13. The roots go to zero, so S is quasinilpotent.

The key obstacle is that S still has many invariant subspaces. In each piece, or fiber, they are the tails, all vectors whose first coordinates are zero. A second operator V commutes with S and moves every tail one step backward[4]. A hyperinvariant subspace would then have to step down forever, which a probability space cannot allow. So the algebra of all maps commuting with S is transitive, meaning it has no common closed invariant subspace except zero and everything[5]. That algebra is also proper and closed under pointwise limits. This answers no to whether every such transitive algebra fills out all operators[6]. Arveson's earlier theorem gave density when the algebra contains a maximal commutative piece[7]. Here that hypothesis fails. The first paper reaches the same conclusion another way. For every irrational angle, it builds a weighted rotation with no nontrivial invariant projection in a standard operator algebra[8]. This answers a question of Zhu, Fang and Shi[10].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal statements for the main results of both papers. They include the operator with a transitive commutant and the rotation counterexample for every irrational angle. So the paper proves these results, as far as the Lean statements match the paper. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: Landmark-level claim with a Lean check of both main constructions. It answers the hyperinvariant-subspace problem only; the ordinary invariant-subspace problem stays open. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A linear map on a Hilbert space that stretches every vector by at most a fixed amount.
A space of vectors, often infinite sequences, with lengths and angles like ordinary space.
A closed flat piece of the space through zero that an operator keeps inside itself.
An invariant subspace that every operator commuting with the given one also keeps inside itself.
The set of all operators A with AT = TA for the given operator T.
An operator whose n-th powers have n-th roots of their norms tending to zero.
A family of operators, closed under sums and products, with no common closed invariant subspace except zero and the whole space.
A projection p, inside a given operator algebra, onto a subspace that the operator keeps inside itself.
